data.analysis: Keep N=3 and the role identities. T1 and T3 both involve tiled CTAs, so distinguish their experiments: T1 uses scratch-backed non-atomic partials and tests hierarchy depth; T3 tests one block-sum atomic per CTA after output initialization. T1 should test, not assume, that one final pass is best. T2 remains an isolated block-reduction comparison, but its implementation may be useful when combined with another hierarchy even if it loses standalone. The only performance evidence is the valid supplied baseline (three samples, mean 47.079 µs); no candidate results are available, so all gains remain hypotheses.

revisions.objective: In src/candidate.cu, compare scratch-backed, non-atomic reduction hierarchies for large n: a coalesced tiled first pass plus one final device sum, and a three-stage or other multistage variant if the partial count makes the final pass costly. Sweep useful per-CTA work and block sizes; do not assume fewer stages always wins. Keep this experiment distinct from T3 by avoiding global atomic output accumulation. Preserve tail safety, scratch bounds, and correctness for every valid input. Validate all required sizes and compare repeated whole-call timings; do not use external DeviceReduce-style libraries.
revisions.subject: Non-atomic reduction hierarchy depth and tile sizing

revisions.objective: Isolate the cost of reduce0's intra-block shared-memory tree: compare a warp-level reduction using valid CUDA sync intrinsics and a correct inter-warp combination, optionally against an allowed CUB block primitive. Hold global input mapping, block geometry, and pass structure fixed during comparisons. Ensure participating lanes use correct masks and synchronization, including tail blocks. Report correctness and repeated whole-call timings. Preserve a correct modular implementation even if it does not beat the full baseline alone, since it may combine differently with a changed hierarchy; do not claim a combination is faster without measuring it.
revisions.subject: Intra-block reduction primitive and synchronization

revisions.objective: Test a one-kernel large-n path: zero out with cudaMemsetAsync on the default stream, then have each CTA reduce its input tile locally and contribute exactly one sum with atomicAdd. Sweep CTA tile size to expose the tradeoff between input work and atomic contention, but avoid per-element atomics and global partial-buffer reduction in this path. Compare the full memset-plus-kernel path with a non-atomic two-kernel control using the same first-pass tile and block mapping, so initialization and finalization costs are visible. Use current input data, no extra allocations, and no stale scratch dependencies; preserve correctness and tail safety for every valid input. Report repeated whole-call timings even if this approach loses.
revisions.subject: Single-kernel atomic finalization with explicit output initialization

data.shared_assumptions: The frozen target is one NVIDIA GH200 with CUDA 12.6.3; the provided baseline is valid and averages 47.079 µs over three samples at n=4,194,304. Its source launches four 128-thread reduction passes at that size, then copies the result device-to-device; this suggests launch and intra-block costs to test, not a proven bottleneck. All candidates must compute from input1 for every valid input, fully produce output on device, obey default-stream ordering, handle tails, and use only the provided scratch with no extra allocations. Compare correct programs using the same whole-call protocol; independently confirm integrated G. The prior version-matched guide check on warp-reduction masks remains relevant: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.6.3/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html
